verses.2: What have you helped one with no strength? What have you strengthened a hand that has no power?
verses.3: What have you advised one with no wisdom? What have you revealed to one who has no insight?
verses.4: To whom have you spoken words? And whose breath has come from you?
verses.5: The dead in the deep tremble, along with those in its dwellings.
verses.6: The realm of the dead is bare before him, and there is no covering for destruction.
verses.7: He stretches the north over emptiness, and hangs the earth on nothing.
verses.8: He binds up the waters in his clouds, and the cloud is not torn open beneath them.
verses.9: He holds back the face of his throne, and hurls his cloud before it.
verses.10: He marks a boundary over the surface of the waters, even to the limit of light with darkness.
verses.11: Pillars of the heavens tremble, and are shaken by his rebuke.
verses.12: By his power he quieted the sea, and by his understanding he struck down Rahab.
verses.13: By his breath the skies are made pure; he pierced the fleeing serpent with his hand.
verses.14: These are but the edges of his ways, and how faint is the whisper of his word! Who can grasp his mighty deeds?

notes:
Notes
- v. 12: "Rahab" is a poetic name for a mythic sea monster; retained as "Rahab" to reflect the Hebrew term (רָהַב).  
- v. 13: "fleeing serpent" (חָנַשׁ) is a poetic image for a hostile force, possibly linked to primordial chaos; "fleeing serpent" reflects the Hebrew verb.
raw:
[1] Then Job answered and said:

[2] What have you helped one with no strength? What have you strengthened a hand that has no power?

[3] What have you advised one with no wisdom? What have you revealed to one who has no insight?

[4] To whom have you spoken words? And whose breath has come from you?

[5] The dead in the deep tremble, along with those in its dwellings.

[6] The realm of the dead is bare before him, and there is no covering for destruction.

[7] He stretches the north over emptiness, and hangs the earth on nothing.

[8] He binds up the waters in his clouds, and the cloud is not torn open beneath them.

[9] He holds back the face of his throne, and hurls his cloud before it.

[10] He marks a boundary over the surface of the waters, even to the limit of light with darkness.

[11] Pillars of the heavens tremble, and are shaken by his rebuke.

[12] By his power he quieted the sea, and by his understanding he struck down Rahab.

[13] By his breath the skies are made pure; he pierced the fleeing serpent with his hand.

[14] These are but the edges of his ways, and how faint is the whisper of his word! Who can grasp his mighty deeds?

---
Notes
- v. 12: "Rahab" is a poetic name for a mythic sea monster; retained as "Rahab" to reflect the Hebrew term (רָהַב).  
- v. 13: "fleeing serpent" (חָנַשׁ) is a poetic image for a hostile force, possibly linked to primordial chaos; "fleeing serpent" reflects the Hebrew verb.
